The seven context window components
To understand context engineering, we need to understand the context window. The context window for language modeling consists of the span of tokens preceding the prompt and the prompt itself. The prompt is usually a sentence, but can also be a longer structure.
GPT-3 was released in 2020 with early context windows of 4, and later upgraded to 200, tokens. By early 2025, those windows were already 2, tokens. The community uses the term context windows, but Andrej Karpathy called context engineering "the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step".
Early context windows were 4, tokens, then upgraded to 200, tokens, before being reduced to 2, tokens.
To understand how context windows work, we need to understand how language models work. The short version is that they learn to predict the next token based on the previous ones. Because context windows grew from 4, to 200, tokens, only to shrink back to 2, tokens, early context engineering focused on prompt engineering. Now, with context windows shrinking, that has shifted to context engineering.
The token budget example comes from a diabetes management coaching agent the author built with LangGraph. The agent is designed to automatically generate conversation structure and explain the next steps to a patient:
The system prompt is one of the seven context window components
The prompt is the most obvious component of the context window, since it’s the task we’re trying to complete. But the other six components also play a role:
- The prompt represents the task we’re trying to complete
- The system prompt is the language model’s representation of the system state. It’s one of seven components that fill the context window
- The goal is the short-term goal
- The perspective is the “who” of the prompt
- The tone is the “how” of the prompt

Context engineering for LLM agents
This post was built with Claude Code, an LLM management framework where agents can spawn subagents and I got 70+ tools to synthesize research papers and technical posts. Technical details below, but first here are the results from the post.
Complicated engineering context for LLM agents is costly
Like most LLM applications, Claude builds and maintains context in a KV-cache between turns. If you’re dealing with JSON, a moderately complex schema with nested objects, descriptions and enums can easily consume 300+ tokens. Here are the stats for the above example.
And the math gets far worse if you hit the call stack limit and spawn subagents. For example, if the patient tools go 4 levels deep, each with 5 tools, you could consume 200 tokens on this one call alone.
Most frontier models claim support for 1-2 million tokens, but I found some evidence suggesting this number is a lie.
First, limited call stack depth means the model’s effective context window is limited to something like 4-10 levels deep. Second, as we increase the token count, we decrease the required model size.
That’s the whole point of cache keys — to keep the number of tokens low for each turn.
The following LongMemEval benchmark showed models given the full ~115, 115-token conversation history performed worse than models given only the relevant subset. This is probably because even with 1 million tokens, explicit cache control and pruning can’t save us from our own artifacts.
Most importantly, 200, 200 tokens appears to be the ceiling for current frontier models, after which output quality degrades substantially.
It’s easy to see why. The state block is 50-100 tokens and the current turn is 100-200 tokens. If you’re making 300 turns, the token costs are 50-100 tokens x 300 turns.
A common mistake is to try and cache everything in a single block and load / unload from disk as you go. Like many problems, this is only worthwhile at scale and at Manus’s scale we have dozens of tools which have to be loaded / unloaded. This turns out to be expensive. For example, if we do 300 turns, it could be 200 tokens x 300 turns.
One alternative is to load and unload more often, but this also turns out to be expensive. For example, if we do 300 turns, it could be 200 tokens x 1 turn.
My recent post on Tool Code explains why these systems are so brittle and easily break the cache prefix.
At Manus’s scale with dozens of tools, cache math probably dominates. The only way we’re going to get past this is by building hybrid models that integrate with custom purpose-built expert agents that can do things like deal with complex schemas, perform deep inference and update persistent state.
This is a promising avenue and it will take time to sort through the many tradeoffs. If you’re building these kinds of systems, I recommend looking at some of my recent posts on hybrid models, search and filtering.
Most frontier models offer explicit cache control with up to 90% discounts on cached input tokens. You can also toggle features like web search, which invalidates the system cache.

In Part 2 we’ll cover retrieval and evaluation in depth. For now let’s keep it simple by looking at 2 examples.
Let’s say the patient is trying to figure out how to use a new insulin pump. In this scenario, the patient profile includes a Type 2 diagnosis. The patient’s first question is “how to use insulin pump” and the tools provide these answers.
In this scenario, the patient profile includes a Type 1 diagnosis. The patient’s first question is “how to use insulin pump” and the tools provide these answers.
Notice the difference is subtle. The first question is “how to use insulin pump” and the answer is correct for a Type 1 patient. The second question is “how to use insulin pump” and the answer is correct for a Type 2 patient. Depending on how you interpret the patient’s first question, the answer could be incorrect. This is where filtering comes in.
In the first scenario, we have 300 turns and 6-10 tools active at each turn. In the second scenario, we have 300 turns and 6-10 tools active at each turn.

The system does not know whether we’re trying to help a Type 1 or Type 2 patient. We assume the same protocol for both types. In this scenario, we need a custom tool that queries the patient profile for a filter condition, gets the answer from the tools, then augments the answer with the condition filter.

The components above are the easy parts. In reality you have a bunch of tools, each of which has its own APIs, schemas and workflows.
The first item on the agenda is to tear apart the tools, which usually looks something like this.
This is where things get really ugly. The tools are now self-contained, event-driven systems with their own state blocks.
Here’s the core problem: we have 6-10 tools active at each turn, each tool has its own internal state and workflows and each tool can have 2-300 turns. After you multiply that out, you end up with 6-10 tools x 6-10 tools x 2-300 turns, which is a big enough context window to make your model slow down, crash or both.

The first solution is to cache everything in a single block and load / unload from disk as you go. For example, if we do 300 turns, it could be 200 tokens x 300 turns.

The problem with this approach is that most of the tools are not critical to the current turn. You may want to keep them for the next couple of turns but past that you can flush them from the context window.
Instead, let’s chop the model into submodels and load / unload them as needed. For example, if we do 300 turns, it could be 200 tokens x 1 turn.
The problem with this approach is that loading and unloading from disk is an expensive operation. In Claude’s case, at Manus’s scale with dozens of tools, cache math probably dominates. The only way we’re going to get past this is by building hybrid models that integrate with custom purpose-built expert agents that can do things like deal with complex schemas, perform deep inference and update persistent state.
The second solution is to call your submodel every turn. For example, if we do 300 turns, it could be 200 tokens x 1 turn.
The problem with this approach is that your submodel has to run through the entire conversation history every turn. The problem with this approach is that your submodels are still in the context window at each turn. In Claude’s case, at Manus’s scale with dozens of tools, cache math probably dominates. Context engineering is a popular approach to improving language model performance. In this post I will describe the engineering strategies we are employing at Manus to condition large language models.
We assume that your large language model is connected to some form of document retriever or information access service. This is not necessary but it is by far the most popular usage pattern.
Strategies
The Manus team employs three strategies for context engineering:
13. Condition on context via prompt engineering
3.13.13.2
Tier one: keep raw context below ~80% capacity
In practice this means we're compacting the sequence every 15-50 tokens. It's fine to briefly surpass 80% capacity, but I aim to start compacting in the 80-90% range, before 95%. We use HuggingFace's CodeAgent to isolate token-heavy objects in sandbox environments, keeping only references in the main context. Other popular frameworks name the four strategies:
LangChain's framework
The Manus team has let agents maintain a file during complex tasks, writing and re-reading their plan. We've found that this counteracts the "lost-in-the-middle" problem across ~50 average tool calls. My agent goes a step further, rewriting the user's message into a self-contained retrieval query before searching. My agent also infers "post-meal readings" from the last 3 turns, an important piece of context for search. Let's look at how my agent rewrote a user query:
This query has almost zero retrieval value because it lacks condition or medication context. My agent adds this information to produce a query that hits relevant documents:
The last step is to condition on this summary via prompt engineering. A query like "My numbers have been all over the place lately" has almost zero retrieval value because it lacks condition or medication context. My agent adds this information to produce a query that hits relevant documents:
The input gate sees only the latest user message and a short classification prompt. The output gate sees only the agent's response and a scope-checking prompt.
3.13.3
Condition on context via prompt engineering
Prompt engineering enables conditioning on context while only exposing the LLM to a small amount of user input. We use OpenAI and Anthropic's production SDKs to trim in atomic turn groups. In practice summarization applies to conversations beyond ~15 turns. We use a similar approach to context engineering as shown above. Our summarization tier fires only when we cannot get below 85% capacity. Our sub-agents return a condensed summary (13, 2, 50 tokens) to the lead agent.
You can read more about our agent here.
3.13.4
This paper found that when you compress instructions and context simultaneously, response quality degrades. Our team is experimenting with various approaches to resolve these issues. The Manus lead agent makes use of a query rewriter that infers the search context from the patient conversation. This rewriter allows us to isolate safety classification into separate LLM calls so that guardrail context does not contaminate the main patient conversation. We also employ a plan file that allows agents to retain knowledge over complex tasks. This counteracts the "lost-in-the-middle" problem across ~50 average tool calls.

Context Distraction
Context distraction is the tendency for models to use their attention budget to focus on irrelevant tokens in a prompt/context instead of the tokens that contain critical information relevant to the task at hand. For example, a Pokemon-playing agent hallucinated an item called "TEA", wrote this into its goals scratchpad, and spent hundreds of actions trying to find it. Clearly, this agent is more concerned with matching the prompt than matching reality.
Source: [100]
Liu et al. documented a similar finding in "Lost-in-the-middle", where they found a consistent U-shaped curve across different models and settings [100]. As the prompt grows beyond ~100, the agent's performance degrades significantly if the relevant information sits in the middle of a long context versus the beginning or end. At 100, the model's attention budget is spread across billions of pair interactions, and critical information gets drowned out.
Chroma calls the mechanism behind context distraction context rot [100], and attributes it to the $O(n^2)$ pairwise token relationships inherent in self-attention. While there are ways to use these relationships more efficiently to increase the capacity of the model, this only improves performance linearly. Beyond ~100, they've noticed agents tend to tend toward repeating actions from history instead of synthesizing novel plans. The author has also noticed this trend, beyond ~100 the model's attention budget is spread too thin to pay attention to everything.
Anthropic's guiding principle is "find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximizes the likelihood of your desired outcome", which minimizes this kind of noise. It's also important to note that this kind of distraction is entirely context-specific, where the same prompt may work fine with one model but fail with another. This makes it hard to detect and even harder to diagnose.
The first example is a direct clash between two conflicting statements that I found during an audit, where I had to use two models to calculate a single token distribution: one model for turning text to text, one model for turning text to numbers.
The agent calls the tool anyway, wasting a round-trip to fetch data that is already in the prompt. The author has caught the agent doing this in several other models, where the fetch tool is still available as a callable tool, contradicting the instruction.
Source: [100]
The second example is a more subtle clash, where the agent calls the tool correctly but calls the wrong tool. The author has caught this in multiple models, and it can be easy to miss as the instruction is in the prompt section but the tool definition is in Python code. In this audit, the agent wrote "TEA" into its goals scratchpad, which is a valid instruction but it's not part of the prompt. For the next hundreds of actions, the agent spends its time trying to find "TEA", which doesn't exist in the game. It's only when it realizes it can't find it that it remembers to do something else.
Source: [100]
The author's own agent had a similar clash, where it spent hundreds of actions trying to follow its instructions without realizing they didn't make any sense. In this case, the agent ended up developing a "black-out strategy", where it intentionally fainted all its Pokemon to teleport.
Source: [100]
The final example is an instruction clash with an external system. The prompt tells the agent to use a patient context if it's already in the prompt, but the system prompt doesn't tell the agent to do this. This is especially common when the agent needs to call a service to get information from that system, e.g. when the agent needs to get the patient's medical history from another system. Here the agent will always re-fetch it, even though the system prompt says "When READING information you already have in the patient context above, use it directly, do not re-fetch with .".
Source: [100]
These are only a few examples of potential context clashes, but the author's experience suggests that there are likely to be more. It's also clear that these clashes are context-specific, i.e. a single model can call the same tool for different tasks. Here the author suggests a few mitigations:
- When building a new model, use diffs to audit for clashes
- When re-using a model, audit for clashes
- When dealing with external systems, use a single shared entrypoint
- When building large models, use an existing prompt from smaller models instead of building it from scratch
- When building a new model, use an existing prompt from smaller models instead of building it from scratch

- If you're re-using a model, audit for clashes

Context engineering in a LangGraph diabetes coaching agent
The agent is a diabetes management coaching assistant built as a ReAct agent using LangGraph. We were tasked with helping optimize the agent's performance on Claude Sonnet.
The diabetes management coaching assistant handles a very wide range of potential topics from flu symptoms to exercise to financial stressors that might affect the patient's ability to manage diabetes. We trained a model that could reference the patient's profile data from the prompt, and the conversation window is char-budgeted at a maximum of 120, 6 turns.
When we first deployed the agent, we noticed that the conversation window was filling up far faster than we expected and we suspected we had a performance issue. We were pretty confident that the agent was referencing the patient's profile data from the prompt, so we began to investigate.
On the first turn, we inject the patient profile into the system prompt (which ranges from ~2, 4 0 0 to ~4 0 0 tokens depending on the session maturity). We were expecting to see the agent reference the patient profile on subsequent turns as well, but we noticed that the agent was referencing the patient profile on nearly every turn. We started to investigate why.
The very first call we made was to our KV-cache. In our prompt, we were referencing the patient's profile data, and we would also specify that the agent should “use the profile in directly”. The KV-cache violation was easy to identify and fix – we were using volatile state prepended to the prompt prefix to invalidate the cache on every turn.
Problem one: KV-cache violation
Removing this tool made the agent more confident in referencing the profile data from the prompt
Problem two: Unnecessary tool fetches
On every turn, we were also fetching the patient profile as a tool. This was causing us to make a redundant fetches, which we were able to resolve by removing the tool entirely (the patient profile is injected into the system prompt on every turn).
The system prompt ranges from ~2, 4 0 0 to ~4 0 0 tokens depending on the session maturity
Removing the redundant fetch resolved problem two, but the conversation window was still filling up far faster than we expected. We started to dig a little deeper, and we noticed that the patient profile was also existing as a callable tool.
Problem three: Redundant tool fetches
We were able to resolve this issue by removing the tool entirely (the patient profile is injected into the system prompt on every turn).
The conversation window holds a maximum of 6 turns, and we were seeing that on nearly every turn, the conversation window was being filled up entirely by the patient profile. We needed to figure out why the patient profile was so long on nearly every turn.
The patient profile is injected into the system prompt on every turn, so we investigated our patient profile tool.
We saw that the tool was being populated from a KV-store, and that the KV-store was being repopulated with new patient data on every turn. In order to do this, we were using a volatile block that changes every turn with the new turn count, new timestamp and new tool history.
Problem four: Volatile state KV
By removing the tool the agent knows it can reference the patient profile directly from the prompt on every turn
The KV-cache violation caused a 10× cost difference between $0. 3 0 /MTok cached vs $3/MTok uncached on Claude Sonnet.
The patient profile was still being written to the conversation window on nearly every turn, but we were able to resolve this issue by removing the tool entirely. The agent now knows that it can reference the patient profile directly from the prompt on every turn.
The patient profile does contain a lot of valuable information, but on nearly every turn, it was not necessary to fetch it. By removing the tool, we were able to resolve problem three and problem four. In doing so, we resolved problem two (the redundant tool fetches) and problem one (the KV-cache violation).

Context engineering is a core task for software engineers. It requires us to fetch the right context for any issue we are addressing – whether that’s understanding a bug fix, figuring out how to implement a new feature, or even discovering the right bugfixes to learn from.
In this blog post, I share my experience with measuring Context-Bench at the time of writing (Fall 43, 2). Context-Bench is a benchmark that tests whether our coding agents can retrieve the right context from 66 real repositories across 8 languages.
Before taking on this task, I had some knowledge of popular LLM approaches, including GPT-300 and GPT-300 but not much in terms of how to assess their performance. Fortunately, my team had already laid the groundwork for me in terms of putting together a baseline model – Claude Sonnet 43.5.
When I started, I was experiencing a KV-cache violation (see Section 5). Once I fixed that, I could directly verify that the improvement was worth it (from ~0% to ~85% on turns 2+).
GPT-5 did turn out to be roughly 77% more expensive than Claude Sonnet 43.5 for slightly lower performance.
I will continue to use Context-Bench for future context engineering tasks, and I hope that others will find this benchmark useful as well.

At one time, an entire industry existed around optimizing Context for storage and cost. It cut expenses on a gigabyte-by-gigabyte basis.
Today, Context can have a different kind of engineering problem.
In heavy agentic workloads, we can get a 100:1 ratio of input tokens to output tokens.
There’s an industry that once existed around optimizing database query planning, network packet routing, and GPU kernel tuning.
They cut expenses on a query-by-query, packet-by-packet, and instruction-by-instruction basis.
Why were those industries so lucrative and how will we tackle this new challenge?
The demand exists.
Given the number of experiments we’ll run, a single prompt ordering mistake can produce a 10× cost difference. Given the number of conversations we’ll have, a 1% input-side optimization can matter more than a 50% output-side optimization.
What works for Claude might fail on GPT or might fail on Gemini.
Every prompt ordering optimization is a successful navigation of a massive combinatorial space.
Do we have the right strategies?
In agent systems, input tokens outnumber output tokens by about 100:1. The context side of the bill dominates.
We’ve spent decades making our storage and computation cheaper.
Do we have the right engineering techniques?
In this new regime, will we need to proactively compress at 80-90% of context capacity? Or will it be better to reactively compress at 95%?
Say we start with Claude - we want to produce more than one output token per input token. Let’s check the numbers.
- Claude compresses at 50% (a high bar)
- Claude doesn’t really compress at all at 100%.
- Claude compresses at 95% (our best shot)
- Claude compresses at 90% (a more feasible shot)
- Claude compresses at 80% (realistically, this is where Claude is already at)
What are our options?
What is the long tail of engineering hacks that allow us to get the full benefit from our existing models?
Say we start with GPT - we want to compress down to zero. Let’s check the numbers.
- GPT compresses at 50% (a low bar, but let’s start here)
